new_statements.quote: Rufiji is to the best of my knowledge not a separate language variety. [...] Following all this, I take Rufiji and Ndengeleko to be the same language. [pp. 14-15] ... There is as yet no analysis of the distribution of tones in Ndengeleko. [...] Odden (1996:3) includes a brief analysis of Ndengeleko tone and concludes that possible contrasts in the position of H tone are highly limited. Surface high pitched syllables have been marked with an acute accent in this work. Following the definition by Hyman (2001): ‘A language with tone is one in which an indication of pitch enters into the lexical realisation of at least some morphemes’, I conclude that this holds for Ndengeleko. [pp. 103-104]

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states a word-stress position for Rufiji. The variety is identified with Ndengeleko, which Ström describes as a tone language (restricted H-tone contrasts per Odden 1996) with no tonal analysis and no word-stress or accent rule; the only occurrence of 'stress' in the phonology is a generic syllable definition quoted from Batibo. Odden 2003 (p. 534, Rufiji-Ruvuma chapter) adds: 'All P-zone languages are tonal (though Ndengereko is losing distinctive prosody under Swahili influence).'
new_statements.exceptions: None; Ström explicitly notes that penultimate vowel lengthening (the usual East Bantu stress correlate) 'is not relevant for Ndengeleko' because the vowel-length contrast is retained (p. 96).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (lexical realisation of morphemes); no phrase-level or citation-form stress statement. Ström's data come from Ndengeleko speakers of the Rufiji and Mkuranga districts, i.e. the same population Ethnologue/ISO label 'Rufiji'.
new_statements.identity_note: rufi1234 is a Glottolog 5.3 Bookkeeping (retired) code with zero references. The only modern first-hand description covering the Rufiji-river population, Ström 2013 (pp. 14-15), states that Rufiji "is to the best of my knowledge not a separate language variety" and "I take Rufiji and Ndengeleko to be the same language", citing Odden 1996:2 ("Rufiji speakers identify themselves as speaking the Rufiji dialect of Ndengereko"). Wikipedia redirects "Rufiji language" to Ndengereko and marks rui as a duplicate code. The language is therefore Ndengeleko/Ndengereko, glottocode nden1248, which is already in the catalog (Ström 2013; tonal-OR-pitch accent, no stress statement). Adding rufi1234 would create a duplicate entity; a retired code does not make a separate language.

sources.note: pp. 14-15: Rufiji is not a separate variety, taken to be the same language as Ndengeleko (citing Odden 1996:2). p. 12: only published material on the variety is Zhukov 1969 'Notes on Kirufiji'. pp. 103-104: tone language per Hyman 2001, no tonal analysis; no word-stress statement anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence: only Batibo's generic syllable definition, p. 101). p. 96: penultimate lengthening not relevant.
